title: Argentina loses bid to halt UK-backed oil exploration near contested Falkland Islands | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

Argentina’srequest to temporarily block UK-authorized oil drilling off the coast of theFalkland Islands– a British overseas territory in the south Atlantic - was rejected by an international court Saturday in a further blow to Argentina’s claim to sovereignty of the islands.

The International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS) ruled 18-3 against Argentina’s request that oil drilling be suspended at the Sea Lion oil field project in the waters off the coast of long-disputed Falkland Islands, which sit around 300 miles east of Argentina’s southeast coast.

Argentinian President Javier Milei had askedthe tribunal to consider the disputeback in October, when he also announced plans to sanction oil companies operating around the islands known in Argentina as Las Malvinas.

Milei perceived the UK’s planned activity as a threat to Argentina’s economy, saying that inaction on his nation’s part would allow the UK to “possess the physical capacity to take the oil reserves that lie beneath our waters.”

He also stressed that permitting the UK to go-ahead with the oilfield project could “create an incentive for the UK to deepen its occupation” and “continue exploiting our resources.”

Argentina had also attempted to prevent Britain from granting further authorizations for the exploitation of maritime resources before the verdict was delivered.

But Britain argued the move would deny Falkland Islanders – a population of roughly 3,500 – the opportunity to develop their natural resources, while also having a “devastating” impact on the territory’s economy.

ITLOS said itdismissed Argentina’s claim because of the ongoing dispute with the UK. The independent tribunal said upholding the claim would be out of its jurisdiction: “This would involve the application of rules of international law lying entirely outside the law of the sea,” the final ruling read.

British Foreign Minister Ed Miliband welcomed Saturday’s ruling allowing the drilling to go ahead.

“This outcome is a vindication of the UK’s robust legal defence and strategy,” the foreign minister said in astatement.

“Argentina sought to stop the Falkland Islanders making their own sovereign decisions and failed in this attempt,” Miliband remarked before urging Argentina to “respect the right of the Falkland Islanders to determine their own future.”

Milei said Argentina would respect the decision of the Hamburg-based tribunal, but vowed that the country would “continue to defend ​its (sovereignty)rights in the framework of international law,” adding: “This decision is not the final word.”

Drilling is slated to begin in March 2027, Britain said, and extraction is expected to commence a year later.

Milei has in recent months ramped up Argentina’s claim to the islands, which have been under UK jurisdiction since 1833 and were the catalyst for a war between the two nations in 1982in which hundreds of lives were lost.

His stancewas boostedafter US President Donald Trump said the US position on the archipelago was “under review.”
